perspective:
I am Ethan Mohamud, a plumber and Gary Guo’s long-time friend from middle school. Gary is a doctor. We have stayed close and rely on each other for emotional and professional support.

I noticed Gary was working excessively long hours at the hospital, often skipping meals and sacrificing sleep. I invited him to a weekend retreat to relax and recover. He told me he appreciated my concern but couldn’t go because there was too much to do at the hospital.

At the retreat, I observed Gary acting restless and avoiding discussions about work. I suspected his overwork was about more than professional obligations. I confronted him, telling him he could tell me anything and that I was there to help, not judge. He said it was complicated and he didn’t want to burden me. He then opened up to me about pressures from managing a new department and personal challenges he was facing. I felt relief and empathy, and offered to help him prioritize tasks, delegate responsibilities, and organize his schedule. He agreed, saying he could use help making time for himself.

Over the following months, I regularly checked in with Gary about his progress and remaining challenges. I saw him making efforts to change. He told me things were better, he was less overwhelmed, and he had time for a movie last weekend. I felt hopeful and proud and continued supporting him.

After a year, I saw that Gary had adjusted to a healthier work-life balance and could manage on his own. I decided to step back but told him I’m always just a call away. He thanked me, said he couldn’t have done it without my support, and said he felt more in control.
